title: Teach us to pray (Luke 11:1–13)
hookLine: the Our Father, a friend at midnight, ask, seek, knock

lines: THE KIDS ARE ASLEEP. GO AWAY.
cards: It's midnight. A friend has shown up after a long trip, hungry, and your kitchen is empty. Not a crust.
So you walk next door and knock. From inside, your neighbor groans: the door's locked, the kids are asleep in the bed with me, I can't get up. You knock again.
Jesus tells this little comedy as his answer to a request from his disciples.

teach.b: Jesus is praying somewhere, and when he stops, one of his disciples says: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." John had given his followers a way to pray. Now Jesus gives his.
Luke's Our Father is shorter than Matthew's, the one Catholics say at Mass. The Catechism notes the difference: Luke gives five petitions, Matthew seven.

Luke's begins simply with Father, then hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, give us our daily bread, forgive us our sins as we forgive, and lead us not into temptation. Then, right away, the midnight friend.
Even if the neighbor won't get up because you're his friend, Jesus says, "yet, because of his importunity, he will rise, and give him as many as he needeth." Importunity means pestering.

The Greek word is bolder: shamelessness. The man gets bread because he won't stop knocking. Then the promise: "Ask, and it shall be given you: seek, and you shall find: knock, and it shall be opened to you."
And one last picture: which father, if his son asks for a fish, hands him a snake?

teach.h: HOW MUCH MORE THE GOOD SPIRIT.
teach.b: If you, imperfect as you are, give good things to your children, how much more will the Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him.

teach.h: KNOCK, AND IT SHALL BE OPENED.
teach.b: Notice where the promise ends: not with whatever you ask for, but with the good Spirit.

how: Catholics pray the Our Father at every Mass and at the start of each decade of the rosary; the Catechism devotes its final section to the prayer, comparing Luke's five petitions with Matthew's seven.

o: an important chance that comes just once
shameless pestering that won't stop asking
a rude visit made at the wrong hour

Luke 11:1. John had taught his own disciples to pray.

games.q: it's midnight, your guest is hungry, and your neighbor says go away, we're all in bed. what does the man in the story do?
o: keep knocking until he gets up.
games.why: he keeps knocking. Jesus says the neighbor gets up because of his importunity, his shameless persistence.

practice: Think of something you asked for once and gave up on: healing for someone, a change in yourself, an answer that never came. Let it come back without embarrassment; the man at midnight wasn't embarrassed.
If you pray, ask again, plainly, and ask for the good Spirit too; if you don't, hold the hope out once more, like a hand raised to knock.

wordCard.voice: importunity. The shameless pestering that got the midnight friend his bread, after the disciples asked Jesus, teach us to pray. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: knock. In Luke, prayer is shameless knocking at the door of a Father who wants to give. That's day four hundred sixty-one.
